chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Faddal, from Ali ibn Uqba, from Musa ibn Uqayl al-Numayri, from Ibn Abi Yafur, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

When the owner of the right is satisfied with the oath of the one who denies his right, and he makes him swear, and he swears that he has no right against him, the oath removes the right of the claimant, so he has no right. I said to him, 'Even if there is a just evidence against him?' He said, 'Yes, and even if he presents it after making him swear fifty oaths by Allah, he has no right, and the oath has invalidated everything he claimed against him that he had made him swear regarding it.'
ai.seo_question: How does an oath by the defendant affect the validity of evidence in Shia Islamic law?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the mechanism of *istihlaf* (compelling an oath), where the defendant's denial under oath effectively extinguishes the plaintiff's claim, even in the presence of prior evidence. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) specifies that fifty oaths (*qasamah*) serve as a comprehensive nullification of the specific rights in dispute, highlighting the weight of the defendant's testimony in Shia jurisprudence. This principle underscores the procedural balance between evidence and sworn denial, a key topic in the chapter on judgment (*al-Hukm wa al-Qada'*).
